summary:
SARWatch is a web application that helps users identify where to investigate possible flooding in Hue, Vietnam. We analyzed NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations from October 15 and 27, 2026, compared candidate changes with Sentinel-2 imagery, and combined them with population and infrastructure data.

Users can explore before-and-after images, inspect the evidence for individual locations, and export a prioritized verification list. We also developed a reproducible processing pipeline and trained a Random Forest model to classify open water.

The project addresses the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge by making radar-observed surface changes easier to examine and interpret. It supports situations where field information and survey resources are limited. It shows missing coverage and conflicting evidence alongside its findings, helping users distinguish possible changes from confirmed flooding. The current application is a research prototype intended to support further investigation.
details:
A satellite change map can highlight unusual conditions, but deciding where to investigate requires more context. Analysts need to know whether a location contains people or essential infrastructure, whether another observation supports the finding, and which parts of the evidence are missing.

We designed the SARWatch tool to provide this information for our case study in Hue, Vietnam. This uses NISAR but includes optical data, population estimates, and mapped infrastructure to allow analysis of specific locations.

The NISAR data (HH and HV) for 15th and 27th October 2026 were registered, invalid data removed, smoothed, and radar power converted to decibels, then used to calculate the change between the two dates.

Otsu thresholding was applied along with decreases in radar power to identify potential water changes. Previous surface water occurrences from JRC and slope from Copernicus DEM were used to filter these changes.

The processing pipeline aligns NISAR HH and HV observations from October 15 and 27, 2026, removes invalid values, smooths radar power before converting it to decibels, and measures changes between the two dates.

Areas of population exposure were estimated by applying WorldPop population data based on the amount of original population cell area overlapping with the candidate area. Road centre lines and critical infrastructure were taken from OpenStreetMap. Areas were then ranked based on direct overlaps with infrastructure, estimated population, road overlaps, and candidate area.

The website allows users to visualise the radar and optical data, understand why an area was prioritised, filter the optical data reference, and download a verification list.

The original analysis contains 1,646 screened candidate regions covering 9.3045 km². A separate repository rerun produces 9.3809 km² after screening. We retain both products and document differences in processing rules and auxiliary inputs.

We also trained a Random Forest using HH, HV, and their difference. On 100,000 held-out pixels from 68 spatial blocks, it achieved an F1 score of 0.8825, compared with 0.8560 for an Otsu baseline. These scores measure agreement with automated Sentinel-2 water labels, not validated flood-detection accuracy

The optical data comparison showed that, of the 1,646 candidates, only 943 had some overlap with clear reference data, and only 9 had any overlap with new optical water. Due to the second optical data being taken ~31.8 hours before NISAR data, we cannot confirm if any areas were flooded during radar data collection.

There was an estimated 1,681 population exposed based on the valid population cells (60.5% of candidate area). There were 18.689 km of mapped roads overlapping.

We used NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, Shapely, PyProj, and scikit-learn for scientific analysis. HTML, CSS, and JavaScript were used for the interface. Node.js was used for data gathering and interface testing. Git and GitHub were used for version control.

Radar subsets were obtained through NASA Earthdata/Harmony, with initial processing on Google Colab. The repository includes the case inputs, trained model, processing scripts, and evaluation records. The historical case can be viewed through a standalone HTML file. Optional rainfall information comes from ECMWF IFS through Open-Meteo.

SARWatch has been designed to make all candidate areas traceable. This means users can understand why the area was chosen, what evidence from independent sources exists, and how the exposure was calculated. Highlighting the lack of evidence or conflicting evidence will help users determine what areas need further investigation.

We considered sensor timing, processing differences, cloud cover, spatial leakage in model evaluation, missing population data, and incomplete infrastructure mapping. The prototype has not been deployed as an operational warning system. Further work requires independent, time-matched flood labels, evaluation across additional events, and feedback from local practitioners.
